danish.title: Anden epilog — Kapitel 6
paragraphs: Kun Guddommens viljesudtryk, uafhængigt af tiden, kan angå en hel serie begivenheder, der strækker sig over år eller århundreder, og kun Guddommen, uafhængig af alt, kan ved Sin vilje alene bestemme retningen for menneskehedens bevægelse; men mennesket handler i tid og deltager selv i det, der sker.
Genopretter vi den første udeladte betingelse, tiden, ser vi, at ingen befaling kan udføres uden en forudgående ordre, der muliggør den sidstes udførelse.

Ingen befaling opstår spontant eller dækker i sig selv en hel serie hændelser; enhver befaling følger af en anden og angår aldrig en hel serie begivenheder, men altid kun ét enkelt øjeblik af en begivenhed.

Når vi for eksempel siger, at Napoleon befalede hære at drage i krig, samler vi i ét samtidigt udtryk en hel serie på hinanden følgende befalinger, der er afhængige af hinanden. Napoleon kunne ikke have befalet en invasion af Rusland og gjorde det aldrig. I dag befalede han, at der skulle skrives visse papirer til Wien, til Berlin og til Petersborg; i morgen visse dekreter og ordrer til hæren, flåden, intendanturet og så videre og så videre — millioner af befalinger, der udgjorde en hel serie, svarende til en serie begivenheder, der førte de franske hære ind i Rusland.

Hvis Napoleon gennem hele sin regeringstid gav befalinger vedrørende en invasion af England og ikke brugte så megen tid og indsats på noget andet foretagende, og dog i hele sin regeringstid aldrig forsøgte at gennemføre denne plan, men i stedet foretog et felttog mod Rusland, som han anså det for ønskeligt at være allieret med (en overbevisning, han gentagne gange udtrykte) — så skyldtes det, at hans befalinger i det første tilfælde ikke svarede til begivenhedernes gang, men i det andet tilfælde gjorde det.

For at en ordre med sikkerhed skal blive udført, er det nødvendigt, at en mand befaler det, der kan udføres. Men at vide, hvad der kan og ikke kan udføres, er umuligt, ikke blot i tilfældet med Napoleons invasion af Rusland, hvori millioner deltog, men selv i den enkleste begivenhed, for i begge tilfælde kan millioner af hindringer opstå, der forhindrer udførelsen. Enhver befaling, der udføres, er altid én af et uhyre antal uudførte. Alle de umulige ordrer, der ikke stemmer med begivenhedernes gang, forbliver uudførte. Kun de mulige knyttes til en sammenhængende serie befalinger, der svarer til en serie begivenheder, og udføres.

Vores fejlagtige forestilling om, at en begivenhed forårsages af en befaling, der går forud for den, skyldes, at når begivenheden har fundet sted, og af tusinder af befalinger de få, der stemte med begivenheden, er blevet udført, glemmer vi de andre, der ikke blev udført, fordi de ikke kunne udføres. Bortset fra det skyldes hovedkilden til vores fejl i denne sag, at den historiske fremstilling generaliserer en hel serie af utallige, mangfoldige og små begivenheder, som for eksempel alle dem, der førte de franske hære til Rusland, til én begivenhed i overensstemmelse med det resultat, denne serie af begivenheder frembragte, og tilsvarende generaliseres hele serien af befalinger også til ét enkelt viljesudtryk.

Vi siger, at Napoleon ønskede at invadere Rusland og invaderede det. I virkeligheden finder vi i hele Napoleons virksomhed aldrig noget, der ligner et udtryk for dette ønske, men en serie ordrer eller viljesudtryk, meget forskelligt og ubestemt rettet. Blandt en lang serie af uudførte ordrer fra Napoleon blev én serie, for felttoget i 1812, gennemført — ikke fordi disse ordrer adskilte sig på nogen måde fra de andre, uudførte ordrer, men fordi de faldt sammen med begivenhedernes gang, der førte den franske hær ind i Rusland; ganske som i stencilarbejde denne eller hin figur fremkommer, ikke fordi farven blev påført fra den ene eller den anden side, men fordi den blev påført fra alle sider over den figur, der var skåret i stencilen.

Undersøger vi altså forholdet i tid mellem befalingerne og begivenhederne, finder vi, at en befaling aldrig kan være årsag til begivenheden, men at der eksisterer en vis bestemt afhængighed mellem de to.

For at forstå, hvori denne afhængighed består, er det nødvendigt at genoprette en anden udeladt betingelse for enhver befaling, der ikke udgår fra Guddommen, men fra et menneske, nemlig at den mand, der giver befalingen, selv deltager i begivenheden.
Denne relation mellem den befalende og dem, han befaler over, er netop det, der kaldes magt. Denne relation består i følgende:

For fælles handling forener mennesker sig altid i bestemte kombinationer, hvori der, uanset forskellen i de mål, der er sat for den fælles handling, altid eksisterer det samme forhold mellem de deltagende.

Mennesker, der forener sig i disse kombinationer, indtager altid sådanne indbyrdes relationer, at det større antal tager en mere direkte del, og det mindre antal en mindre direkte del i den fælles handling, de har forenet sig om.
Af alle de kombinationer, hvori mennesker forener sig for fælles handling, er en af de mest slående og tydelige eksempler en hær.

Enhver hær består af de laveste grader — menige — af hvem der altid er flest; af den næste højere militære grad — korporaler og underofficerer — af hvem der er færre; og af endnu højere officerer, af hvem der er endnu færre, og så fremdeles op til den øverste militære kommando, der er samlet i én person.

En militær organisation kan ganske rigtigt sammenlignes med en kegle, hvis basis med den største diameter består af de menige; det næste højere og smallere snit af keglen består af de næste højere grader i hæren, og så videre til spidsen, hvis punkt repræsenterer den øverstbefalende.

Soldaterne, som der er flest af, udgør keglens nedre sektion og dens basis. Det er soldaten selv, der stikker, hugger, brænder og plyndrer, og han modtager altid ordrer til disse handlinger fra mænd over ham; han giver selv aldrig en ordre. Underofficererne (som der er færre af) udfører selv handlingen sjældnere end soldaterne, men de giver allerede befalinger. En officer handler endnu sjældnere direkte selv, men befaler endnu hyppigere. En general gør intet andet end at befale over tropperne, angiver målet og bruger næsten aldrig selv et våben. Den øverstbefalende deltager aldrig direkte i selve handlingen, men giver kun almene ordrer om bevægelsen af troppemasserne. Et lignende forhold mellem mennesker ses i enhver kombination af mennesker for fælles virksomhed — i landbrug, handel og enhver forvaltning.

Og uden at analysere alle de sammenhængende snit af en kegle og graderne i en hær eller rangene og positionerne i nogen som helst administrativ eller offentlig virksomhed fra de laveste til de højeste, ser vi en lov, ifølge hvilken mennesker, der forener sig til fælles handling, kombineres på en sådan måde, at jo mere direkte de deltager i handlingens udførelse, desto mindre kan de befale og desto flere er de, mens jo mindre direkte de deltager i selve handlingen, desto mere befaler de og desto færre er de; stigende på denne måde fra de laveste grader til den mand på toppen, der tager den mindste direkte del i handlingen og hovedsagelig retter sin virksomhed mod at befale.
Dette forhold mellem de befalende og dem, de befaler over, er det, der udgør kernen i begrebet magt.

Genopretter vi tidsbetingelsen, under hvilken alle begivenheder finder sted, finder vi, at en befaling kun udføres, når den er forbundet med en tilsvarende serie begivenheder. Genopretter vi den væsentlige betingelse om forholdet mellem de befalende og de udførende, finder vi, at de, der befaler, ifølge sagens natur tager den mindste del i selve handlingen, og at deres virksomhed udelukkende er rettet mod at befale.

english.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Only the expression of God's will, which is independent of time, can relate to a whole series of events spanning years or centuries, and only God, independent of everything, can by His will alone determine the direction of humanity's movement. But a human being acts in time and is himself part of events.

Restoring the first condition that was left out—the element of time—we see that no command can be carried out unless some prior command has already been given that makes the execution of the latest one possible.

No command ever appears out of nowhere or covers an entire series of events by itself; each command follows from another, and each always relates to one specific moment of an event, never to a whole series.

When we say, for instance, that Napoleon ordered armies to go to war, we are combining in one simultaneous expression a whole series of consecutive commands that depended on one another. Napoleon could not have commanded an invasion of Russia and never did so. One day he ordered certain papers to be written to Vienna, to Berlin, and to Petersburg; the next day he ordered certain decrees and instructions to the army, the fleet, and the commissariat, and so on and so on—millions of commands making up a series of commands corresponding to a series of events that brought the French army to Russia.

If throughout his reign Napoleon issued commands about an invasion of England—spending more time and effort on that project than on any other—yet during his whole reign never once attempted it, and instead invaded Russia, with which he considered it advantageous to be allied, this was because the first set of commands did not and could not correspond to the course of events, while the second set did.

For an order to be reliably carried out, a person must command what can actually be done. But knowing what can and what cannot be done is impossible—not only in the case of Napoleon's invasion of Russia, where millions of people participated, but even in the simplest event—because in either case millions of obstacles may arise. Every order executed is always one of an immense number unexecuted. All the impossible orders inconsistent with the course of events remain unexecuted. Only the possible ones get linked up with a consecutive series of commands corresponding to a series of events, and are executed.

Our mistaken belief that an event is caused by the command that precedes it comes from the fact that, after the event has taken place, out of thousands of commands only those few that happened to match the event are remembered as having been carried out. We forget about the others because they didn't match the event and therefore weren't executed. Apart from that, the chief source of our error in this matter is due to the fact that in the historical accounts a whole series of innumerable, diverse, and petty events, such for instance as all those which led the French armies to Russia, is generalized into one event in accord with the result produced by that series of events, and corresponding with this generalization the whole series of commands is also generalized into a single expression of will.

We say that Napoleon wanted to invade Russia and invaded it. In reality, throughout Napoleon's entire career we never find anything resembling an expression of that desire. What we find is a series of commands—expressions of his will—that are enormously varied and vaguely directed. Out of Napoleon's countless series of unexecuted orders, one series—for the campaign of 1812—was carried out, not because those particular orders differed in any way from the ones that weren't, but because they happened to coincide with the course of events that led the French army into Russia. Just as a stencil doesn't produce the image on a wall because paint was applied from this side or that, but because paint was applied from all sides of the stencil's cut-out shape.
So, examining the relationship between commands and events in time, we find that a command can never be the cause of an event, but that a definite interdependence exists between the two.

To understand what this interdependence consists of, it is necessary to restore another condition that was left out of every command—a condition that applies to commands issued by human beings, not by God: the person who gives the command is himself a participant in the event.
This relationship of the commander to those he commands is precisely what is called power. This relationship consists in the following:

For collective action, people always combine into certain groups, and in these groups—regardless of the differences in the goals set for the collective action—the relationship between participants is always the same.

People who unite in these groups always relate to one another in such a way that the greater number take a more direct part, and the smaller number take a less direct part, in the collective action they have joined together to perform.
Of all the groups in which people combine for collective action, one of the most clear-cut and well-defined examples is an army.

Every army is made up of the lowest ranks—the ordinary soldiers—of whom there are always the most; of the next higher rank—corporals and non-commissioned officers, of whom there are fewer; of still higher officers, of whom there are fewer yet; and so on up to the highest military command, which is concentrated in a single person.

A military organization can be precisely compared to a cone, whose base—the widest part—consists of the rank and file; the next section, narrower and higher, consists of the next grades of the army; and so on to the apex of the cone, which represents the commander-in-chief.

The soldiers, who are the most numerous, form the lowest section and the base of the cone. The ordinary soldier does the actual fighting—the stabbing, hacking, burning, and looting—and always receives his orders from those above him; he never gives orders himself. The non-commissioned officers (of whom there are fewer) less often perform the actual fighting than the soldiers, but they do give orders. An officer still more rarely takes direct part in the action, and gives orders more frequently. A general does nothing but command troops, indicate the objective, and hardly ever uses a weapon himself. The commander-in-chief never takes direct part in the action at all, and only makes general plans for the movement of the masses. A similar relationship exists among people who combine for any kind of collective action—in commerce, in government, in every human enterprise.

And so, without analyzing in detail every section of the cone and every rank and position in any administrative or public enterprise from the lowest to the highest, we see a law by which people combine to take collective action in relationships such that the more directly they participate in carrying out the action, the less they can direct it, and the more they direct, the less they directly participate. The proportion rises from the soldiers at the base of the cone to its single apex—the supreme commander, who takes the least direct part in the action and devotes his activity primarily to commanding.
This relationship of the people who command to those who carry out the commands is what constitutes the essence of the concept called power.

Having restored the condition of time—under which all events occur—we find that a command is only carried out when it corresponds to an actual series of events. Restoring the essential condition of the relationship between those who command and those who execute, we find that by the very nature of the case, those who command take the least direct part in the event itself, and that their activity is devoted exclusively to commanding.
